title: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every pair versus a greedy bit trie walk.

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums, find the maximum possible value of nums[i] XOR nums[j] over every pair of indices i and j.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Two Most Contrasting Light Patterns
blocks.text: Like comparing every pair of light patterns from a set of switch panels and finding the pair that differs in the most positions at once, since XOR rewards positions where the two patterns disagree.

blocks.caption: Find the pair of numbers whose XOR produces the largest possible value

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["5 (00101) XOR 25 (11001) equals 28 (11100)","no other pair produces a larger XOR","5 and 25 differ at the two most significant bits among all values present, which XOR rewards the most heavily"],["Answer","28","28 is the maximum XOR achievable from any pair in this array"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["14 (001110) XOR 70 (1000110) equals 92 (1011100)","the only pair available","With exactly two numbers, there is only one possible pair, so its XOR is automatically the maximum"],["Answer","92","The single available pair's XOR is trivially both the minimum and the maximum"]]}

blocks.text: Both values being identical means their XOR is always 0, so the answer is 0.

Before comparing every pair, notice what actually makes an XOR value large: XOR rewards disagreement, and disagreement at a more significant bit position matters far more than disagreement at every less significant one combined.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A bit that differs between two numbers contributes 1 to that bit position of their XOR, and a 1 at a more significant position outweighs any combination of 1s at every less significant position, just like 1000 in binary already beats 0111.

Observation 2: So maximizing XOR is fundamentally a greedy, most-significant-bit-first decision: for a fixed number, its ideal partner is whichever available number disagrees with it at the highest possible bit position, then the next highest, and so on.

Observation 3: Comparing every pair directly answers this question correctly but wastefully, since it never reuses the bit-level structure shared between numbers; a data structure organized by bit prefix, a binary trie, lets that greedy decision be made directly.

Observation 4: Inserting every number into a trie by its bits from most significant to least significant, then walking the trie for each number always preferring the branch representing the opposite bit, reconstructs the greedy answer directly without ever comparing two full numbers against each other explicitly.

Whenever a problem asks to maximize (or minimize) a bitwise combination across pairs, think most-significant-bit-first greedy choice, and consider a bit trie as the data structure that makes that greedy choice efficient.

This same greedy, bit-by-bit mindset is what several other bit manipulation problems build on, and the trie here plays the same role that a hash map plays in value-based lookup problems, just organized by bit prefix instead of by exact value.
Check every pair of numbers directly, computing their XOR and tracking the largest one found.

items: For every pair of indices i and j, compute nums[i] XOR nums[j].
Keep the largest XOR value found across every pair.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The inner loop starts at j = i + 1, so each unordered pair is compared exactly once instead of twice, and a number is never XORed against itself.
best = max(best, ...) / Math.max(best, ...) keeps only the running maximum seen so far, since only the single largest XOR value across all pairs is needed, not every individual result.
Every pair is genuinely compared, with no early exit, since there is no way to know in advance which pair will produce the true maximum without a structure-free approach checking them all.

blocks.text: Every pair's XOR is directly computed, so the true maximum is guaranteed to be found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), checking every pair.
Space: O(1) extra, no additional structure is used.

Limitation: maximizing XOR is really about greedily choosing, at every bit position from the most significant down, the value that disagrees with the current number, and checking every pair explicitly does not take advantage of that structure at all.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force's real waste is repeatedly asking the same kind of question, "what is this number's best XOR partner", from scratch for every single pair, throwing away any structure discovered while answering it for one number before moving on to the next. But a number's best XOR partner is determined entirely by its own bits, checked from the most significant one down, against whichever other numbers share or differ at each prefix. If every number's bits were pre-organized into a shared structure indexed by bit prefix, a binary trie, answering "what is this number's best partner" becomes a single greedy walk down the trie, always preferring the branch for the opposite bit when it exists. Building that trie once costs O(32n), and then finding the best partner for every one of the n numbers costs another O(32n), replacing the O(n squared) pairwise comparison with two linear-in-n passes.

Insert every number's binary representation, one bit at a time from the most significant bit down, into a binary trie. Then, for every number, walk the trie trying at each level to go toward the child representing the opposite bit value (since a differing bit at a more significant position always produces a larger XOR), falling back to the same bit's child only if the opposite one does not exist. This greedily finds the best possible XOR partner for each number directly from the trie.
Build a bit trie of every number, then greedily walk it for each number seeking the opposite bit at every level.
Dry run for nums = [5, 25] (binary 00101, 11001, using 5 bits for clarity)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Insert 00101 and 11001 into the trie, bit by bit from the most significant","both paths exist in the trie","Every number's bits are laid out along a root-to-leaf path, so any two numbers sharing a bit prefix also share that portion of the path"],["Walking for 00101: at the first bit (0), try to go to the opposite child (1)","the 11001 path has a 1 here, take it","A differing bit at the most significant position is worth more than agreeing at every other position, so the opposite branch is always preferred when it exists"],["Continuing greedily at every remaining level, always preferring the opposite bit when available","ends up matched against 11001 entirely","At every level the walk keeps choosing disagreement over agreement whenever both are possible, which is exactly the greedy maximization rule"],["Resulting XOR","00101 XOR 11001 = 11100 = 28","The greedy walk reconstructs the actual XOR value one bit at a time as it descends the trie"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: a bit trie lets each number greedily find its best XOR partner

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times 32), inserting and querying each number through a fixed depth trie.
Space: O(n times 32), for the trie nodes in the worst case.

Because more significant bits always outweigh the combined value of every less significant bit, choosing the locally best (opposite) bit at each level from most significant to least significant is also globally optimal: no later, lower-significance decision could ever compensate for a worse choice made earlier at a higher bit position.

blocks.content: {"headers":["At each trie level","Effect on the resulting XOR"],"rows":[["Opposite bit exists and is taken","That bit position contributes its full value (1 shifted to that position) to the XOR"],["Opposite bit does not exist, same bit taken instead","That bit position contributes 0 to the XOR, since both numbers agree there"]]}

items: highest_bit (or the fixed 31 in Java and C++) fixes how many levels the trie needs, so every number is inserted using the exact same bit ordering, from most significant to least significant.
insert walks down creating a new TrieNode only when the current bit's child does not already exist, so numbers sharing a prefix reuse the same nodes.

best_xor / findMaximumXOR's second loop, for every bit from most significant to least significant, checks whether the opposite bit's child exists; if it does, that bit is set in result and the walk continues down the opposite branch, otherwise it falls back to the same bit's child.
Every number is inserted before any number is queried, since a number's best partner might appear anywhere else in the array, including at a later index.

blocks.text: The bit trie approach directly encodes the greedy insight that maximizing XOR means preferring a differing bit at the most significant position possible, and this same trie based greedy walk technique generalizes to variants of this problem involving range constraints or online queries.

items: Forgetting to insert all numbers into the trie before querying any of them, which would miss potential partners that appear later in the array.
Walking the trie preferring the same bit instead of the opposite one, which defeats the entire purpose of maximizing XOR and instead minimizes it.
Using a bit depth that is too shallow for the actual range of input values, silently truncating the more significant bits of larger numbers and producing an incorrect maximum.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["Only two numbers in the array","Reduces to a single direct XOR computation either way, since there is exactly one pair"],["All numbers identical","Every possible XOR is 0, correctly reflected by the trie walk always landing back on the same bit's child since no opposite bit is ever available"]]}

items: Mention the alternative bitmask prefix technique (building the answer bit by bit from the most significant bit down using a hash set of number prefixes) as an equally valid technique achieving the same complexity without an explicit trie structure, useful if a trie feels too heavyweight to implement under time pressure.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Maximize (or minimize) some bitwise combination over every pair" points toward a most-significant-bit-first greedy choice, implemented either with a binary trie over bit prefixes or an equivalent hash set of prefixes checked bit by bit.

items: How would you support this query repeatedly as numbers are added to the array over time? Insert each new number into the trie as it arrives, and query it against the existing trie immediately, an online version of the same greedy walk.

Can you find the maximum XOR for a pair restricted to a specific numeric range or subarray? This typically needs a different structure, such as a persistent trie or an offline sorted-query approach, since a plain trie has no notion of index or range.

What is the alternative to a trie that achieves the same complexity? Build the answer bit by bit from the most significant bit down, at each step testing a candidate prefix against a hash set of all numbers' prefixes so far, without ever building an explicit tree structure.
Same greedy, most-significant-bit-first mindset as constructing the smallest or largest number achievable under bitwise constraints, one bit at a time.
The bit trie itself is the same core data structure used in word-search-style prefix tries, just keyed by binary digits instead of alphabet characters.
Same "find the best partner using a bit prefix hash set" fallback technique appears in various maximum or minimum XOR subarray, and maximum-XOR-with-constraint variants of this problem.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (bit trie with greedy walk): O(n times 32) time, O(n times 32) space.

items: Pattern: Greedy most-significant-bit-first XOR maximization via a binary trie
Core Idea: A bit trie organizes every number by its bit prefix, so each number's best XOR partner can be found by always preferring the opposite bit at each level, from most significant to least
Time: O(32n), effectively O(n)
Space: O(32n), effectively O(n), for the trie nodes
Most Important Observation: A more significant differing bit always outweighs every less significant bit combined, making a greedy, level-by-level trie walk both simple and globally optimal
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Chase the opposite bit, top bit first
